claims.text: The initially solid nanoparticles are equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloys with diameters of 5–20 nm.
Nanoscale surface chemical heterogeneity governs the premelting and melting behavior of equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Cu preferentially segregates to the surfaces of these nanoparticles.
Preferential surface Cu segregation locally depresses the melting point.
Preferential surface Cu segregation broadens the melting transition relative to a chemically homogeneous particle.
A surface-enrichment treatment can increase the Cu concentration in the outer 1–2 nm shell relative to an untreated randomized ensemble.
Localized surface Cu enrichment lowers the Gibbs free energy for surface disordering.
Localized surface Cu enrichment lowers the Gibbs free energy for nucleating a premelted layer.
The reduced free-energy barrier causes surface-driven melting to begin at a lower temperature.
The reduced free-energy barrier causes melting to proceed over a broader temperature range.
Particles with enhanced surface Cu will begin surface premelting tens of kelvins below randomized baseline particles.
Particles with enhanced surface Cu will have a broader melting interval than randomized baseline particles.
The proposed mechanism applies to equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles between approximately 5 and 20 nm in diameter.
The proposed mechanism may not hold for particles larger than 20 nm.
The proposed mechanism may not hold for particles with heavy surface oxidation.
A mild anneal with reducing-agent exposure will induce Cu surface segregation.
